claim: Dihydroceramide desaturases convert dihydroceramides to ceramides, the precursors of all complex sphingolipids.
source: Dihydroceramide desaturases convert dihydroceramides to ceramides, the precursors of all complex sphingolipids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the enzymatic function of dihydroceramide desaturases in sphingolipid biosynthesis.

claim: Reduction of DEGS1 dihydroceramide desaturase function causes pediatric neurodegenerative disorder hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-18 (HLD-18).
source: Reduction of DEGS1 dihydroceramide desaturase function causes pediatric neurodegenerative disorder hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-18 (HLD-18).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this disease association.

claim: infertile crescent (ifc) is the Drosophila DEGS1 homolog.
source: We discovered that infertile crescent (ifc), the Drosophila DEGS1 homolog, is expressed primarily in glial cells to promote CNS development by guarding against neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is established by sequence homology and functional conservation between ifc and DEGS1.

claim: ifc is expressed primarily in glial cells.
source: We discovered that infertile crescent (ifc), the Drosophila DEGS1 homolog, is expressed primarily in glial cells to promote CNS development by guarding against neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is supported by RNA in situ hybridization and transcriptional reporter data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of ifc causes massive dihydroceramide accumulation.
source: Loss of ifc causes massive dihydroceramide accumulation and severe morphological defects in cortex glia, including endoplasmic reticulum (ER) expansion, failure of neuronal ensheathment, and lipid droplet depletion.
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data showing increased dihydroceramide levels in ifc mutants.

claim: Loss of ifc causes severe morphological defects in cortex glia, including endoplasmic reticulum (ER) expansion.
source: Loss of ifc causes massive dihydroceramide accumulation and severe morphological defects in cortex glia, including endoplasmic reticulum (ER) expansion, failure of neuronal ensheathment, and lipid droplet depletion.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and TEM imaging data showing ER expansion in ifc mutant cortex glia.

claim: Loss of ifc causes failure of neuronal ensheathment by cortex glia.
source: Loss of ifc causes massive dihydroceramide accumulation and severe morphological defects in cortex glia, including endoplasmic reticulum (ER) expansion, failure of neuronal ensheathment, and lipid droplet depletion.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing that cortex glia fail to enwrap neuronal cell bodies in ifc mutants.

claim: Loss of ifc causes lipid droplet depletion in cortex glia.
source: Loss of ifc causes massive dihydroceramide accumulation and severe morphological defects in cortex glia, including endoplasmic reticulum (ER) expansion, failure of neuronal ensheathment, and lipid droplet depletion.
evidence: This is supported by BODIPY staining and TEM imaging showing reduced lipid droplets in ifc mutant cortex glia.

claim: RNAi knockdown of the upstream ceramide synthase schlank in glia of ifc mutants rescues ER expansion.
source: RNAi knockdown of the upstream ceramide synthase schlank in glia of ifc mutants rescues ER expansion, suggesting dihydroceramide accumulation in the ER drives this phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence and TEM data showing reduced ER expansion when schlank is knocked down in glia of ifc mutants.

claim: Dihydroceramide accumulation in the ER drives ER expansion in ifc mutants.
source: RNAi knockdown of the upstream ceramide synthase schlank in glia of ifc mutants rescues ER expansion, suggesting dihydroceramide accumulation in the ER drives this phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of ER expansion by reducing dihydroceramide synthesis through schlank knockdown.

claim: RNAi knockdown of ifc in glia but not neurons drives neuronal cell death.
source: RNAi knockdown of ifc in glia but not neurons drives neuronal cell death, suggesting that ifc function in glia promotes neuronal survival.
evidence: This is supported by Cleaved Caspase-3 staining showing neuronal cell death when ifc is knocked down specifically in glia.

claim: ifc function in glia promotes neuronal survival.
source: RNAi knockdown of ifc in glia but not neurons drives neuronal cell death, suggesting that ifc function in glia promotes neuronal survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that glial-specific ifc knockdown causes neuronal cell death.

claim: Glia are the primary site of disease progression in HLD-18.
source: Our work identifies glia as the primary site of disease progression in HLD-18 and may inform on juvenile forms of ALS, which also feature elevated dihydroceramide levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings that ifc acts primarily in glia and that glial dysfunction drives neurodegeneration.

claim: Juvenile forms of ALS feature elevated dihydroceramide levels.
source: Our work identifies glia as the primary site of disease progression in HLD-18 and may inform on juvenile forms of ALS, which also feature elevated dihydroceramide levels.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on juvenile ALS and sphingolipid metabolism.

claim: Sphingolipids are enriched in glial cells, comprising up to 30% of all membrane lipids in oligodendrocytes.
source: Sphingolipids are key structural and functional components of the cell membrane in all eukaryotic cells and are enriched in glial cells, such as oligodendrocytes, where they comprise up to 30% of all membrane lipids (Jackman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: All complex sphingolipids derive from ceramide.
source: All complex sphingolipids, like glycosylsphingolipids and sphingomyelin, derive from ceramide (Ghosh et al., 2013; Vacaru et al., 2013; Hannun and Obeid, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about sphingolipid biosynthesis supported by citations.

claim: Dihydroceramide desaturases produce ceramide from dihydroceramide by catalyzing the formation of a trans double bond between carbons 4 and 5 of the sphingoid backbone.
source: In the de novo ceramide biosynthesis pathway, dihydroceramide desaturases, such as DEGS1, produce ceramide from dihydroceramide by catalyzing the formation of a trans double bond between carbons 4 and 5 of the sphingoid backbone, which enhances conformational plasticity (Li et al., 2002; Yasuda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the enzymatic mechanism supported by citations.

claim: The trans double bond between carbons 4 and 5 of the sphingoid backbone enhances conformational plasticity.
source: In the de novo ceramide biosynthesis pathway, dihydroceramide desaturases, such as DEGS1, produce ceramide from dihydroceramide by catalyzing the formation of a trans double bond between carbons 4 and 5 of the sphingoid backbone, which enhances conformational plasticity (Li et al., 2002; Yasuda et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on ceramide structure and function.

claim: Bi-allelic mutations in DEGS1 cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-18 (HLD-18).
source: In humans, bi-allelic mutations in DEGS1 cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-18 (HLD-18), a progressive, often fatal pediatric neurodegenerative disease marked by cerebral atrophy, white matter reduction, and hypomyelination (Dolgin et al., 2019; Karsai et al., 2019; Pant et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical literature.

claim: HLD-18 is a progressive, often fatal pediatric neurodegenerative disease marked by cerebral atrophy, white matter reduction, and hypomyelination.
source: In humans, bi-allelic mutations in DEGS1 cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy-18 (HLD-18), a progressive, often fatal pediatric neurodegenerative disease marked by cerebral atrophy, white matter reduction, and hypomyelination (Dolgin et al., 2019; Karsai et al., 2019; Pant et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical literature.

claim: The primary neural cell type impacted by loss of DEGS1 function is unknown.
source: The primary neural cell type impacted by loss of DEGS1 function and the cell biology of how disruption of ceramide synthesis leads to neurodegeneration remain unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the manuscript aims to address.

claim: The cell biology of how disruption of ceramide synthesis leads to neurodegeneration remains unknown.
source: The primary neural cell type impacted by loss of DEGS1 function and the cell biology of how disruption of ceramide synthesis leads to neurodegeneration remain unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the manuscript aims to address.

claim: The de novo ceramide biosynthetic pathway is well conserved among higher metazoans.
source: The de novo ceramide biosynthetic pathway is well conserved among higher metazoans (Hannun and Obeid, 2018; Fyrst et al., 2004; Acharya and Acharya, 2005; Dunn et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on comparative biochemistry.

claim: De novo ceramide synthesis occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: De novo ceramide synthesis occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and starts with the rate-limiting activity of the serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) complex, which condenses serine and palmitoyl-CoA (lauoryl-CoA in flies) to form 3-Ketosphinganine, which is converted to sphinganine by 3-Ketosphinganine reductase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the subcellular location of ceramide biosynthesis.

claim: The serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) complex catalyzes the rate-limiting step of de novo ceramide synthesis.
source: De novo ceramide synthesis occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and starts with the rate-limiting activity of the serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) complex, which condenses serine and palmitoyl-CoA (lauoryl-CoA in flies) to form 3-Ketosphinganine, which is converted to sphinganine by 3-Ketosphinganine reductase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ceramide biosynthesis.

claim: The SPT complex condenses serine and palmitoyl-CoA (lauryl-CoA in flies) to form 3-Ketosphinganine.
source: De novo ceramide synthesis occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and starts with the rate-limiting activity of the serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) complex, which condenses serine and palmitoyl-CoA (lauoryl-CoA in flies) to form 3-Ketosphinganine, which is converted to sphinganine by 3-Ketosphinganine reductase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the enzymatic reaction catalyzed by SPT.

claim: 3-Ketosphinganine is converted to sphinganine by 3-Ketosphinganine reductase.
source: De novo ceramide synthesis occurs in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and starts with the rate-limiting activity of the serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) complex, which condenses serine and palmitoyl-CoA (lauoryl-CoA in flies) to form 3-Ketosphinganine, which is converted to sphinganine by 3-Ketosphinganine reductase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ceramide biosynthesis.

claim: Ceramide synthases condense sphinganine with acyl-CoA to generate dihydroceramide.
source: Ceramide synthases condense sphinganine with acyl-CoA to generate dihydroceramide, which is converted to ceramide by dihydroceramide desaturases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ceramide biosynthesis.

claim: Dihydroceramide is converted to ceramide by dihydroceramide desaturases.
source: Ceramide synthases condense sphinganine with acyl-CoA to generate dihydroceramide, which is converted to ceramide by dihydroceramide desaturases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ceramide biosynthesis.

claim: Ceramide is transported from the ER to the Golgi by the specific ceramide transporter CERT.
source: Ceramide is then efficiently transported by the specific ceramide transporter CERT from the ER to the Golgi (Kumagai et al., 2005), where it undergoes headgroup modifications to produce complex sphingolipids that eventually translocate to the plasma membrane (Kobayashi and Menon, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on ceramide trafficking.

claim: Ceramide undergoes headgroup modifications in the Golgi to produce complex sphingolipids.
source: Ceramide is then efficiently transported by the specific ceramide transporter CERT from the ER to the Golgi (Kumagai et al., 2005), where it undergoes headgroup modifications to produce complex sphingolipids that eventually translocate to the plasma membrane (Kobayashi and Menon, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on sphingolipid biosynthesis.

claim: Complex sphingolipids eventually translocate to the plasma membrane.
source: Ceramide is then efficiently transported by the specific ceramide transporter CERT from the ER to the Golgi (Kumagai et al., 2005), where it undergoes headgroup modifications to produce complex sphingolipids that eventually translocate to the plasma membrane (Kobayashi and Menon, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on sphingolipid trafficking.

claim: Mutations in most members of the SPT complex, ceramide synthases, and DEGS1 lead to neurodegeneration.
source: Mutations in most members of the SPT complex, ceramide synthases, and DEGS1 lead to neurodegeneration (Hannun and Obeid, 2018; Dunn et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2023), identifying the de novo ceramide biosynthesis pathway as a hotspot for neurodegenerative disease mutations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: The de novo ceramide biosynthesis pathway is a hotspot for neurodegenerative disease mutations.
source: Mutations in most members of the SPT complex, ceramide synthases, and DEGS1 lead to neurodegeneration (Hannun and Obeid, 2018; Dunn et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2023), identifying the de novo ceramide biosynthesis pathway as a hotspot for neurodegenerative disease mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple genes in this pathway are associated with neurodegeneration.

claim: Reduction or loss of DEGS1 function in human patients or cell lines, mice, zebrafish, and flies drives dihydroceramide accumulation and ceramide depletion.
source: Consistent with its central role in ceramide biogenesis, reduction or loss of DEGS1 function in human patients or cell lines, mice, zebrafish, and flies drives dihydroceramide accumulation and ceramide depletion (Karsai et al., 2019; Pant et al., 2019; Holland et al., 2007; Jung et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature across multiple model systems.

claim: HLD-18 patients display reduced myelin sheath thickness in peripheral nerves.
source: HLD-18 patients display reduced myelin sheath thickness in peripheral nerves, and knockdown of DEGS1 function in zebrafish reduces the number of myelin basic protein-positive oligodendrocytes (Karsai et al., 2019; Pant et al., 2019), suggesting DEGS1 regulates Schwann cell and oligodendrocyte development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical literature.

claim: Knockdown of DEGS1 function in zebrafish reduces the number of myelin basic protein-positive oligodendrocytes.
source: HLD-18 patients display reduced myelin sheath thickness in peripheral nerves, and knockdown of DEGS1 function in zebrafish reduces the number of myelin basic protein-positive oligodendrocytes (Karsai et al., 2019; Pant et al., 2019), suggesting DEGS1 regulates Schwann cell and oligodendrocyte development.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on zebrafish models.

claim: DEGS1 regulates Schwann cell and oligodendrocyte development.
source: HLD-18 patients display reduced myelin sheath thickness in peripheral nerves, and knockdown of DEGS1 function in zebrafish reduces the number of myelin basic protein-positive oligodendrocytes (Karsai et al., 2019; Pant et al., 2019), suggesting DEGS1 regulates Schwann cell and oligodendrocyte development.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed effects of DEGS1 loss on myelinating cells.

claim: Genetic ablation of ifc drives activity-dependent photoreceptor degeneration in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, genetic ablation of infertile crescent (ifc), the fly DEGS1 ortholog, drives activity-dependent photoreceptor degeneration (Jung et al., 2017), suggesting that ifc function is crucial for neuronal homeostasis.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature on ifc in Drosophila.

claim: ifc function is crucial for neuronal homeostasis.
source: In Drosophila, genetic ablation of infertile crescent (ifc), the fly DEGS1 ortholog, drives activity-dependent photoreceptor degeneration (Jung et al., 2017), suggesting that ifc function is crucial for neuronal homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of ifc causes photoreceptor degeneration.

claim: Forced expression of a wild-type ifc transgene in neurons, glia, or muscles was shown to rescue the ifc mutant phenotype.
source: In addition, forced expression of a wild-type ifc transgene in neurons, glia, or muscles was shown to rescue the ifc mutant phenotype (Jung et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Whether ifc/DEGS1 acts primarily in glia, neurons, or other cells to regulate nervous system development remains to be determined.
source: Whether ifc/DEGS1 acts primarily in glia, neurons, or other cells to regulate nervous system development then remains to be determined.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the manuscript aims to address.

claim: Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of ceramide synthase function suppresses the reduction of MBP-positive oligodendrocytes in zebrafish caused by DEGS1 deficiency.
source: Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of ceramide synthase function, which should reduce dihydroceramide levels, suppresses the observed reduction of MBP-positive oligodendrocytes in zebrafish and the activity-dependent photoreceptor degeneration in flies triggered by reduction of DEGS1/ifc function (Pant et al., 2019; Jung et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of ceramide synthase function suppresses activity-dependent photoreceptor degeneration in flies caused by ifc deficiency.
source: Pharmacological or genetic inhibition of ceramide synthase function, which should reduce dihydroceramide levels, suppresses the observed reduction of MBP-positive oligodendrocytes in zebrafish and the activity-dependent photoreceptor degeneration in flies triggered by reduction of DEGS1/ifc function (Pant et al., 2019; Jung et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Gain of function mutations in components of the SPT complex cause juvenile amyotrophic lateral sclerosis due to elevated sphingolipid biosynthesis.
source: Dihydroceramide accumulation may also contribute to other neurodegenerative diseases, as gain of function mutations in components of the SPT complex cause juvenile amyotrophic lateral sclerosis due to elevated sphingolipid biosynthesis, with dihydroceramides showing the greatest relative increase of all sphingolipids (Lone et al., 2022; Lone et al., 2023; Syeda et al., 2024; Dohrn et al., 2024; Srivastava et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature on juvenile ALS.

claim: In juvenile ALS caused by SPT mutations, dihydroceramides show the greatest relative increase of all sphingolipids.
source: Dihydroceramide accumulation may also contribute to other neurodegenerative diseases, as gain of function mutations in components of the SPT complex cause juvenile amyotrophic lateral sclerosis due to elevated sphingolipid biosynthesis, with dihydroceramides showing the greatest relative increase of all sphingolipids (Lone et al., 2022; Lone et al., 2023; Syeda et al., 2024; Dohrn et al., 2024; Srivastava et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature on juvenile ALS.

claim: How dihydroceramide accumulation alters the cell biology of neurons, glia, or both to trigger myelination defects and neurodegeneration is unclear.
source: How dihydroceramide accumulation alters the cell biology of neurons, glia, or both to trigger myelination defects and neurodegeneration is unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the manuscript aims to address.

claim: Drosophila is a powerful system to dissect the genes and pathways that regulate glial development and function.
source: With its vast genetic toolkit, Drosophila is a powerful system in which to dissect the genes and pathways that regulate glial development and function (Freeman and Doherty, 2006; Coutinho-Budd and Freeman, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on Drosophila as a model system.

claim: In flies, six morphologically and functionally distinct glial subtypes regulate nervous system development and homeostasis.
source: In flies, six morphologically and functionally distinct glial subtypes regulate nervous system development and homeostasis (Yildirim et al., 2019; Corty and Coutinho-Budd, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on Drosophila glia.

claim: Perineurial and subperineurial glia act as physiochemical barriers to protect the nervous system and control metabolite exchange with the hemolymph.
source: The surface perineurial and subperineurial glia act as physiochemical barriers to protect the nervous system and control metabolite exchange with the hemolymph, carrying out a similar function as the human blood–brain barrier (Stork et al., 2008; Volkenhoff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on Drosophila glia.

claim: Perineurial and subperineurial glia carry out a similar function as the human blood-brain barrier.
source: The surface perineurial and subperineurial glia act as physiochemical barriers to protect the nervous system and control metabolite exchange with the hemolymph, carrying out a similar function as the human blood–brain barrier (Stork et al., 2008; Volkenhoff et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on Drosophila glia.

claim: Cortex glia ensheathe the cell bodies of neuroblasts and neurons in the CNS in protective, nutritive, honeycomb-like membrane sheaths.
source: Residing between the surface glia and the neuropil, cortex glia ensheathe the cell bodies of neuroblasts and neurons in the CNS in protective, nutritive, honeycomb-like membrane sheaths.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cortex glia function in Drosophila.

claim: Ensheathing glia define the boundary of the neuropil and insulate axons, dendrites, and synapses from neuronal cell bodies in the CNS.
source: Ensheathing glia define the boundary of the neuropil and insulate axons, dendrites, and synapses from neuronal cell bodies in the CNS (Freeman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature on Drosophila glia.

claim: Astrocyte-like glia extend fine membrane protrusions that infiltrate the neuropil and form a meshwork of cellular processes that ensheathe synapses and regulate synaptic homeostasis in the CNS.
source: Astrocyte-like glia extend fine membrane protrusions that infiltrate the neuropil and form a meshwork of cellular processes that ensheathe synapses and regulate synaptic homeostasis in the CNS (Freeman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature on Drosophila glia.

claim: Wrapping glia reside internally to the surface glia and insulate axons in the PNS to enhance neuronal signaling and provide energy support.
source: In the PNS, wrapping glia reside internally to the surface glia and insulate axons in the PNS to enhance neuronal signaling and provide energy support.
evidence: This is established knowledge about wrapping glia function in Drosophila.

claim: ifc acts primarily in glia to regulate CNS development.
source: Using the Drosophila model, we found that ifc acts primarily in glia to regulate CNS development, with its loss disrupting glial morphology.
evidence: This is supported by gene rescue and RNAi experiments showing that ifc function in glia is necessary and sufficient for CNS development.

claim: Loss of ifc disrupts glial morphology.
source: Using the Drosophila model, we found that ifc acts primarily in glia to regulate CNS development, with its loss disrupting glial morphology.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing morphological defects in multiple glial subtypes in ifc mutants.

claim: Inappropriate accumulation and retention of dihydroceramide in the ER drives ER expansion, glial swelling, and the failure of glia to enwrap neurons.
source: Our work supports a model in which inappropriate accumulation and retention of dihydroceramide in the ER drives ER expansion, glial swelling, and the failure of glia to enwrap neurons, ultimately leading to neuronal degeneration as a secondary consequence of glial dysfunction.
evidence: This model is supported by lipidomics, microscopy, and genetic rescue data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neuronal degeneration in ifc mutants occurs as a secondary consequence of glial dysfunction.
source: Our work supports a model in which inappropriate accumulation and retention of dihydroceramide in the ER drives ER expansion, glial swelling, and the failure of glia to enwrap neurons, ultimately leading to neuronal degeneration as a secondary consequence of glial dysfunction.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that glial-specific ifc knockdown causes neuronal cell death.

claim: The findings on ifc likely illuminate the mechanism through which elevated dihydroceramide levels drive neuronal degeneration and cell death in flies and humans.
source: Given the conserved nature of de novo ceramide biosynthesis, our findings likely illuminate the exact mechanism through which elevated dihydroceramide levels drive neuronal degeneration and cell death in flies and humans.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of the ceramide biosynthesis pathway and the similarity of phenotypes across species.

claim: ifcjs1 and ifcjs2 encode V276D and G257S missense mutations, respectively.
source: Whole-genome sequencing revealed that ifc was independently mutated in each line: ifcjs1 and ifcjs2 encode V276D and G257S missense mutations, respectively, and ifcjs3 encodes a W162* nonsense mutation (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by whole-genome sequencing data.

claim: ifcjs3 encodes a W162* nonsense mutation.
source: Whole-genome sequencing revealed that ifc was independently mutated in each line: ifcjs1 and ifcjs2 encode V276D and G257S missense mutations, respectively, and ifcjs3 encodes a W162* nonsense mutation (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by whole-genome sequencing data.

claim: The ifc allele encodes an E241K missense mutation.
source: Sanger sequencing also uncovered a missense mutation, E241K, in the molecularly uncharacterized ifc (Jackman et al., 2009) allele (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Sanger sequencing data.

claim: All four ifc mutations reside in the fatty acid desaturase domain.
source: All four mutations reside in the fatty acid desaturase domain, the hotspot for mutations in human DEGS1 that cause HLD-18 (Figure 1B, B').
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and comparison to human DEGS1 mutations shown in Figure 1B and B'.

claim: The fatty acid desaturase domain is the hotspot for mutations in human DEGS1 that cause HLD-18.
source: All four mutations reside in the fatty acid desaturase domain, the hotspot for mutations in human DEGS1 that cause HLD-18 (Figure 1B, B').
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical literature and shown in Figure 1B'.

claim: Loss of ifc function results in a near complete loss of ceramides in the CNS and whole larvae.
source: Loss of ifc function resulted in a near complete loss of ceramides and a commensurate increase in dihydroceramides in the CNS and whole larvae (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of ifc function results in a commensurate increase in dihydroceramides in the CNS and whole larvae.
source: Loss of ifc function resulted in a near complete loss of ceramides and a commensurate increase in dihydroceramides in the CNS and whole larvae (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sphinganine exhibits a significant increase in its levels in the absence of ifc function.
source: Sphinganine, the metabolite directly upstream of dihydroceramide, also exhibited a significant increase in its levels in the absence of ifc function, while metabolites further upstream were unchanged in abundance or undetectable (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Metabolites upstream of sphinganine were unchanged in abundance or undetectable in ifc mutants.
source: Sphinganine, the metabolite directly upstream of dihydroceramide, also exhibited a significant increase in its levels in the absence of ifc function, while metabolites further upstream were unchanged in abundance or undetectable (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ceramide derivatives like sphingosine, CPE, and glucosyl-ceramide (Gl-Cer) were reduced in levels in ifc mutants.
source: Ceramide derivatives like sphingosine, CPE, and glucosyl-ceramide (Gl-Cer) were reduced in levels and replaced by their cognate dihydroceramide forms (e.g., Glc-DiCer) (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ceramide derivatives were replaced by their cognate dihydroceramide forms in ifc mutants.
source: Ceramide derivatives like sphingosine, CPE, and glucosyl-ceramide (Gl-Cer) were reduced in levels and replaced by their cognate dihydroceramide forms (e.g., Glc-DiCer) (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In ifc−/− larvae, there is a clear reduction in Dpn-positive neuroblasts in the optic lobe.
source: In ifc−/− larvae, we observed a clear reduction in Dpn-positive neuroblasts in the optic lobe, swelling of glia in peripheral nerves, enhanced RFP expression in the CNS, and the presence of large swollen, cortex glia identified by RFP labeling and FABP expression (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5.

claim: In ifc−/− larvae, there is swelling of glia in peripheral nerves.
source: In ifc−/− larvae, we observed a clear reduction in Dpn-positive neuroblasts in the optic lobe, swelling of glia in peripheral nerves, enhanced RFP expression in the CNS, and the presence of large swollen, cortex glia identified by RFP labeling and FABP expression (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In ifc−/− larvae, there is enhanced RFP expression in the CNS.
source: In ifc−/− larvae, we observed a clear reduction in Dpn-positive neuroblasts in the optic lobe, swelling of glia in peripheral nerves, enhanced RFP expression in the CNS, and the presence of large swollen, cortex glia identified by RFP labeling and FABP expression (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: In wild-type larvae, cortex glia display compact cell bodies and fully enwrap individual neuronal cell bodies with their membrane sheaths.
source: In wild-type larvae, cortex glia display compact cell bodies and fully enwrap individual neuronal cell bodies with their membrane sheaths (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 4; Kis et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and by citation to prior literature.

claim: In ifc−/− larvae, cortex glia display swollen cell bodies.
source: In ifc−/− larvae, cortex glia display swollen cell bodies, fail to fully enwrap neuronal cell bodies, displace neurons from their regular arrangement, and appear to contain brightly fluorescent RFP-positive aggregates (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: In ifc−/− larvae, cortex glia fail to fully enwrap neuronal cell bodies.
source: In ifc−/− larvae, cortex glia display swollen cell bodies, fail to fully enwrap neuronal cell bodies, displace neurons from their regular arrangement, and appear to contain brightly fluorescent RFP-positive aggregates (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In ifc−/− larvae, cortex glia displace neurons from their regular arrangement.
source: In ifc−/− larvae, cortex glia display swollen cell bodies, fail to fully enwrap neuronal cell bodies, displace neurons from their regular arrangement, and appear to contain brightly fluorescent RFP-positive aggregates (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In ifc−/− larvae, cortex glia appear to contain brightly fluorescent RFP-positive aggregates.
source: In ifc−/− larvae, cortex glia display swollen cell bodies, fail to fully enwrap neuronal cell bodies, displace neurons from their regular arrangement, and appear to contain brightly fluorescent RFP-positive aggregates (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Loss of ifc function affects all CNS glial subtypes except perineurial glia.
source: Using this approach, we determined that loss of ifc function affects all CNS glial subtypes except perineurial glia (Figure 2E, E', J, J').
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In ifc mutants, cortex glia appear swollen, fail to enwrap neurons, and accumulate large amounts of Myr-GFP+ internal membranes.
source: Cortex glia appeared swollen, failed to enwrap neurons, and accumulated large amounts of Myr-GFP+ internal membranes (Figure 2A, A', F, F').
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A, A', F, F'.

claim: In ifc mutants, ensheathing glia display swollen, disorganized cell bodies and accumulate Myr-GFP+ internal membranes.
source: Ensheathing glia (Figure 2B, B', G, G'), and subperineurial glia (Figure 2D, D', I, I') also displayed swollen, disorganized cell bodies and accumulated Myr-GFP+ internal membranes.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2B, B', G, G'.

claim: In ifc mutants, subperineurial glia display swollen, disorganized cell bodies and accumulate Myr-GFP+ internal membranes.
source: Ensheathing glia (Figure 2B, B', G, G'), and subperineurial glia (Figure 2D, D', I, I') also displayed swollen, disorganized cell bodies and accumulated Myr-GFP+ internal membranes.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2D, D', I, I'.

claim: In ifc mutants, astrocyte-like glia display smaller cell bodies, reduced membrane extensions, and disrupted organization along the dorsal–ventral nerve cord.
source: Astrocyte-like glia displayed smaller cell bodies, reduced membrane extensions, and disrupted organization along the dorsal–ventral nerve cord (Figure 2C, C').
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2C, C'.

claim: The number of subperineurial glia is unchanged between wild-type and ifc−/− larvae.
source: The number of subperineurial glia was unchanged between the two genotypes, but we observed a 12%, 40%, and 72% reduction in the number of astrocyte-like, ensheathing, and cortex glia, respectively, in ifc−/− larvae relative to wild-type (Figure 2K–N).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2N.

claim: There is a 12% reduction in the number of astrocyte-like glia in ifc−/− larvae relative to wild-type.
source: The number of subperineurial glia was unchanged between the two genotypes, but we observed a 12%, 40%, and 72% reduction in the number of astrocyte-like, ensheathing, and cortex glia, respectively, in ifc−/− larvae relative to wild-type (Figure 2K–N).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: There is a 40% reduction in the number of ensheathing glia in ifc−/− larvae relative to wild-type.
source: The number of subperineurial glia was unchanged between the two genotypes, but we observed a 12%, 40%, and 72% reduction in the number of astrocyte-like, ensheathing, and cortex glia, respectively, in ifc−/− larvae relative to wild-type (Figure 2K–N).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: There is a 72% reduction in the number of cortex glia in ifc−/− larvae relative to wild-type.
source: The number of subperineurial glia was unchanged between the two genotypes, but we observed a 12%, 40%, and 72% reduction in the number of astrocyte-like, ensheathing, and cortex glia, respectively, in ifc−/− larvae relative to wild-type (Figure 2K–N).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: A reduction in cell proliferation contributes to the observed reduction in the number of cortex glia in ifc mutants.
source: Subsequent experiments revealed that a reduction in cell proliferation and an increase in apoptosis both contribute to the observed reduction in the number of cortex glia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: An increase in apoptosis contributes to the observed reduction in the number of cortex glia in ifc mutants.
source: Subsequent experiments revealed that a reduction in cell proliferation and an increase in apoptosis both contribute to the observed reduction in the number of cortex glia (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pan-glial, but not pan-neuronal, knockdown of ifc recapitulates the swollen cortex glia phenotype observed in ifc mutant larvae.
source: Focusing on FABP-positive cortex glia due to their easily scorable phenotype, we found that pan-glial, but not pan-neuronal, knockdown of ifc recapitulated the swollen cortex glia phenotype observed in ifc mutant larvae (Figure 3C, D, J).
evidence: This is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments and microscopy data shown in Figure 3C, D, J.

claim: Only pan-glial DEGS1 expression provides rescuing activity, albeit at much weaker levels than the Drosophila ifc transgene.
source: Identical experiments using the human DEGS1 transgene revealed that only pan-glial DEGS1 expression provided rescuing activity, albeit at much weaker levels than the Drosophila ifc transgene (Figure 3G, I, K).
evidence: This is supported by gene rescue experiments and microscopy data shown in Figure 3G, I, K.

claim: Pan-glial expression of the Drosophila ifc transgene is ~15-fold more potent than the human DEGS1 transgene at rescuing the ifc lethal phenotype to adulthood.
source: Pan-glial expression of the Drosophila ifc transgene was, in fact, ~15-fold more potent than the human DEGS1 transgene at rescuing the ifc lethal phenotype to adulthood: When ifc was expressed in all glia, 57.9% of otherwise ifc mutant flies survived to adulthood (n = 2452), but when ifc was replaced by DEGS1 only 3.9% of otherwise ifc mutant flies reached adulthood (n = 1303).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of adult survival in gene rescue experiments.

claim: When ifc is expressed in all glia, 57.9% of otherwise ifc mutant flies survive to adulthood.
source: Pan-glial expression of the Drosophila ifc transgene was, in fact, ~15-fold more potent than the human DEGS1 transgene at rescuing the ifc lethal phenotype to adulthood: When ifc was expressed in all glia, 57.9% of otherwise ifc mutant flies survived to adulthood (n = 2452), but when ifc was replaced by DEGS1 only 3.9% of otherwise ifc mutant flies reached adulthood (n = 1303).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of adult survival in gene rescue experiments.

claim: When DEGS1 is expressed in all glia, only 3.9% of otherwise ifc mutant flies reach adulthood.
source: Pan-glial expression of the Drosophila ifc transgene was, in fact, ~15-fold more potent than the human DEGS1 transgene at rescuing the ifc lethal phenotype to adulthood: When ifc was expressed in all glia, 57.9% of otherwise ifc mutant flies survived to adulthood (n = 2452), but when ifc was replaced by DEGS1 only 3.9% of otherwise ifc mutant flies reached adulthood (n = 1303).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of adult survival in gene rescue experiments.

claim: No ifc mutant larvae reach adulthood in the absence of either ifc or DEGS1 transgene.
source: No ifc mutant larvae reached adulthood in the absence of either transgene (n = 1030).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of adult survival in control experiments.

claim: Human DEGS1 can partially substitute for ifc function in flies despite a difference in the preferred length of the sphingoid backbone in flies versus mammals.
source: We infer that ifc acts primarily in glia to govern CNS development and that human DEGS1 can partially substitute for ifc function in flies despite a difference in the preferred length of the sphingoid backbone in flies versus mammals (Fyrst et al., 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the partial rescue of ifc mutant phenotypes by human DEGS1 expression, supported by citation to prior literature on sphingoid backbone differences.

claim: elav-GAL4 drives UAS-linked transgene expression not just in neurons, but also in glia at appreciable levels.
source: In this context, we note that elav-GAL4 drives UAS-linked transgene expression not just in neurons, but also in glia at appreciable levels (Berger et al., 2007; Lacin et al., 2024) and thus needs to be paired with repo-GAL80 to restrict GAL4-mediated gene expression to neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on elav-GAL4 expression patterns.

claim: elav-GAL4 needs to be paired with repo-GAL80 to restrict GAL4-mediated gene expression to neurons.
source: In this context, we note that elav-GAL4 drives UAS-linked transgene expression not just in neurons, but also in glia at appreciable levels (Berger et al., 2007; Lacin et al., 2024) and thus needs to be paired with repo-GAL80 to restrict GAL4-mediated gene expression to neurons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the GAL4/GAL80 system in Drosophila.

claim: ifc is widely expressed in the CNS.
source: RNA in situ hybridization revealed that ifc is widely expressed in the CNS (Figure 4A), most obviously in the distinctive star-shaped astrocyte-like glia (Figure 4B), which are marked by Ebony expression (Ziegler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ifc is most obviously expressed in the distinctive star-shaped astrocyte-like glia.
source: RNA in situ hybridization revealed that ifc is widely expressed in the CNS (Figure 4A), most obviously in the distinctive star-shaped astrocyte-like glia (Figure 4B), which are marked by Ebony expression (Ziegler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by RNA in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The ifc-T2A-GAL4 transcriptional reporter shows strong expression in astrocyte-like glia.
source: Thus, we paired the ifc-T2A-GAL4 transcriptional reporter with a nuclear RFP (nRFP) transgene (He et al., 2019) and confirmed authenticity of the ifc-T2A-GAL4 line by its strong expression in astrocyte-like glia (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The ifc-T2A-GAL4 transcriptional reporter shows strong nRFP expression in all glial cells and modest nRFP expression in all neurons.
source: Using this approach, we observed strong nRFP expression in all glial cells and modest nRFP expression in all neurons (Figure 4D, E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting ifc is transcribed at higher levels in glial cells than neurons in the larval CNS.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4D, E, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: ifc is transcribed at higher levels in glial cells than neurons in the larval CNS.
source: Using this approach, we observed strong nRFP expression in all glial cells and modest nRFP expression in all neurons (Figure 4D, E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting ifc is transcribed at higher levels in glial cells than neurons in the larval CNS.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential expression levels of the ifc-T2A-GAL4 reporter in glia versus neurons.

claim: Ifc-GFP colocalizes strongly with the ER markers Calnexin 99A (CNX99A) and ESYT.
source: Using a fosmid transgene that harbors a GFP-tagged version of ifc flanked by ~36 kb of its endogenous genomic region and molecular markers for ER, cis-Golgi, and trans-Golgi (Sarov et al., 2016; Bergeron et al., 1994; Kikuma et al., 2017; Park et al., 2022), we found that the Ifc-GFP colocalized strongly with the ER markers Calnexin 99A (CNX99A) and ESYT (Figure 4F, F', G, G', Figure 1—figure supplement 7) and weakly with the cis-Golgi marker GOLGIN84 and the trans-Golgi marker GOLGIN245 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization microscopy data shown in Figure 4F, F', G, G'.

claim: Ifc-GFP colocalizes weakly with the cis-Golgi marker GOLGIN84 and the trans-Golgi marker GOLGIN245.
source: Using a fosmid transgene that harbors a GFP-tagged version of ifc flanked by ~36 kb of its endogenous genomic region and molecular markers for ER, cis-Golgi, and trans-Golgi (Sarov et al., 2016; Bergeron et al., 1994; Kikuma et al., 2017; Park et al., 2022), we found that the Ifc-GFP colocalized strongly with the ER markers Calnexin 99A (CNX99A) and ESYT (Figure 4F, F', G, G', Figure 1—figure supplement 7) and weakly with the cis-Golgi marker GOLGIN84 and the trans-Golgi marker GOLGIN245 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ifc localizes primarily to the ER.
source: Our results indicate that Ifc localizes primarily to the ER, aligning with the presumed site of de novo ceramide biosynthesis and prior work on DEGS1 localization in cell lines (Karsai et al., 2019; Kawano et al., 2006).
evidence: This is inferred from the colocalization data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Loss of ifc causes a clear expansion of the ER marker CNX99A in cortex glia.
source: Focusing on cortex glia, we observed a clear expansion of the ER marker CNX99A (Figure 4H, H', K, K'), a mild enrichment of the Golgi markers, GOLGIN84 and GOLGIN245, in diffuse 'clouds' (Figure 4I, I', L, L', Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and a reduction in expression of the lysosome marker LAMP (Figure 4J, J', M, M') in ifc−/− larvae.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4H, H', K, K'.

claim: Loss of ifc causes a mild enrichment of the Golgi markers, GOLGIN84 and GOLGIN245, in diffuse 'clouds' in cortex glia.
source: Focusing on cortex glia, we observed a clear expansion of the ER marker CNX99A (Figure 4H, H', K, K'), a mild enrichment of the Golgi markers, GOLGIN84 and GOLGIN245, in diffuse 'clouds' (Figure 4I, I', L, L', Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and a reduction in expression of the lysosome marker LAMP (Figure 4J, J', M, M') in ifc−/− larvae.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4I, I', L, L', and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of ifc causes a reduction in expression of the lysosome marker LAMP in cortex glia.
source: Focusing on cortex glia, we observed a clear expansion of the ER marker CNX99A (Figure 4H, H', K, K'), a mild enrichment of the Golgi markers, GOLGIN84 and GOLGIN245, in diffuse 'clouds' (Figure 4I, I', L, L', Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and a reduction in expression of the lysosome marker LAMP (Figure 4J, J', M, M') in ifc−/− larvae.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4J, J', M, M'.

claim: In wild-type, cortex glia display a compact cytoplasm that surrounds a large nucleus.
source: In wild-type, cortex glia display a compact cytoplasm that surrounds a large nucleus (Figure 5A, B) and extend glial sheaths that fully enwrap adjacent neuronal cell bodies (black arrows; Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: In wild-type, cortex glia extend glial sheaths that fully enwrap adjacent neuronal cell bodies.
source: In wild-type, cortex glia display a compact cytoplasm that surrounds a large nucleus (Figure 5A, B) and extend glial sheaths that fully enwrap adjacent neuronal cell bodies (black arrows; Figure 5C, D).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5C, D.

claim: In ifc−/− larvae, cortex glia display enlarged cell bodies with a maze-like pattern of internal membranes.
source: In ifc−/− larvae, cortex glia display enlarged cell bodies with a maze-like pattern of internal membranes (solid white arrows; Figure 5A', B', E, E') and fail to enwrap neurons (hollow white arrows; Figure 5C', D').
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5A', B', E, E'.

claim: In ifc−/− larvae, cortex glia fail to enwrap neurons.
source: In ifc−/− larvae, cortex glia display enlarged cell bodies with a maze-like pattern of internal membranes (solid white arrows; Figure 5A', B', E, E') and fail to enwrap neurons (hollow white arrows; Figure 5C', D').
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5C', D'.

claim: The internal membrane structures in ifc mutant cortex glia appear to assume an ER-like identity.
source: The internal membrane structures appear to assume an ER-like identity, as we observed significant overlap between the ER marker CNX99A and the membrane marker Myr-GFP when Myr-GFP was driven by a cortex glia-specific GAL4 line (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization microscopy data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Loss of ifc causes similar yet milder effects on cell swelling and internal membrane accumulation in subperineurial and wrapping glia in abdominal nerves.
source: We observed similar yet milder effects on cell swelling and internal membrane accumulation in subperineurial and wrapping glia in abdominal nerves purple and pink shading, respectively (Figure 5G, G', H, H'), indicating that loss of ifc drives internal membrane accumulation in and swelling of multiple glial subtypes.
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5G, G', H, H'.

claim: Loss of ifc drives internal membrane accumulation in and swelling of multiple glial subtypes.
source: We observed similar yet milder effects on cell swelling and internal membrane accumulation in subperineurial and wrapping glia in abdominal nerves purple and pink shading, respectively (Figure 5G, G', H, H'), indicating that loss of ifc drives internal membrane accumulation in and swelling of multiple glial subtypes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of similar phenotypes across multiple glial subtypes.

claim: TEM analysis reveals a near complete depletion of lipid droplets in the CNS of ifc−/− larvae.
source: TEM analysis also revealed a near complete depletion of lipid droplets in the CNS of ifc−/− larvae (compare Figure 5A, C, D–A', C', D'; lipid droplets marked by asterisk; Figure 5M), which we confirmed using BODIPY to mark neutral lipids in FABP-positive cortex glia (Figure 5I–L).
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 5A, C, D, A', C', D', M and BODIPY staining data shown in Figure 5I–L.

claim: In the CNS, lipid droplets form primarily in cortex glia.
source: In the CNS, lipid droplets form primarily in cortex glia (Kis et al., 2015) and are thought to contribute to membrane lipid synthesis through their catabolism into free fatty acids versus acting as an energy source in the brain (Grabner et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Lipid droplets are thought to contribute to membrane lipid synthesis through their catabolism into free fatty acids versus acting as an energy source in the brain.
source: In the CNS, lipid droplets form primarily in cortex glia (Kis et al., 2015) and are thought to contribute to membrane lipid synthesis through their catabolism into free fatty acids versus acting as an energy source in the brain (Grabner et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Loss of ifc drives transcriptional upregulation of genes that promote membrane lipid biogenesis, such as SREBP, SCAP, and Pcyt1/Pcyt2.
source: Consistent with the possibility that increased membrane lipid synthesis drives lipid droplet reduction, RNA-seq assays of dissected nerve cords revealed that loss of ifc drove transcriptional upregulation of genes that promote membrane lipid biogenesis, such as SREBP, the conserved master regulator of lipid biosynthesis, SCAP, an activator of SREBP, and Pcyt1/Pcyt2, which promote phosphatidylcholine (PC) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) synthesis (Eberlé et al., 2004; Osborne and Espenshade, 2009; Jacquemyn et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data and citations to prior literature on these genes.

claim: The spliced form of Xbp-1 mRNA (Xbp-1s) is upregulated in the CNS of ifc mutant larvae.
source: The spliced form of Xbp-1 mRNA (Xbp-1s) (Figure 5J), which promotes membrane lipid synthesis required for ER biogenesis and is activated by the unfolded protein response (UPR) (Sriburi et al., 2007), is also upregulated in the CNS of ifc mutant larvae.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Most ER chaperones are downregulated in ifc mutant larvae.
source: Most ER chaperones, which are typically transcriptionally upregulated upon UPR activation (Bernales et al., 2006), were however downregulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that in this case, misfolded protein is not the factor that triggers UPR activation and increased ER membrane biogenesis upon loss of ifc.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Misfolded protein is not the factor that triggers UPR activation and increased ER membrane biogenesis upon loss of ifc.
source: Most ER chaperones, which are typically transcriptionally upregulated upon UPR activation (Bernales et al., 2006), were however downregulated (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that in this case, misfolded protein is not the factor that triggers UPR activation and increased ER membrane biogenesis upon loss of ifc.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ER chaperones are downregulated despite UPR activation.

claim: There is a five- and threefold drop in TG levels in the CNS and whole larvae of ifc mutant larvae relative to wild-type.
source: Lipid droplets are composed largely of triacylglycerols (TGs), Jacquemyn et al., 2017 and we observed a five- and threefold drop in TG levels in the CNS and whole larvae of ifc mutant larvae relative to wild-type (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Lipidomics analysis reveals a shift of TGs toward higher saturation levels in the absence of ifc function.
source: Our lipidomics analysis also revealed a shift of TGs toward higher saturation levels in the absence of ifc function (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: There is transcriptional upregulation of most genes in the Lands cycle in ifc mutants.
source: Consistent with this, we observed transcriptional upregulation of most genes in the Lands cycle, which remodels phospholipids by replacing existing fatty acyl groups with new fatty acyl groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Moessinger et al., 2014; Moessinger et al., 2011; Harayama et al., 2014; O'Donnell, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the absence of ifc function, PC and PE exhibit little change in quantity.
source: In the absence of the ifc function, PC and PE exhibited little change in quantity (Figure 6D, G), but the levels of the less abundant PS were increased threefold in the CNS of ifc mutant larvae relative to wild-type (compare Figure 6J to Figure 6D, G).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 6D, G.

claim: The levels of PS are increased threefold in the CNS of ifc mutant larvae relative to wild-type.
source: In the absence of the ifc function, PC and PE exhibited little change in quantity (Figure 6D, G), but the levels of the less abundant PS were increased threefold in the CNS of ifc mutant larvae relative to wild-type (compare Figure 6J to Figure 6D, G).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: PC, PE, and PS display increased saturation levels in ifc mutants.
source: All three phospholipids, however, displayed increased saturation levels: The relative levels of all PC, PE, and PS species were reduced, except for the most saturated form of each phospholipid – 18:1/18:1 – which is increased (Figure 6E, F, H–L).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 6E, F, H–L.

claim: The relative levels of all PC, PE, and PS species are reduced in ifc mutants, except for the most saturated form of each phospholipid – 18:1/18:1 – which is increased.
source: All three phospholipids, however, displayed increased saturation levels: The relative levels of all PC, PE, and PS species were reduced, except for the most saturated form of each phospholipid – 18:1/18:1 – which is increased (Figure 6E, F, H–L).
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 6E, F, H–L.

claim: The increase in saturation of PC, PE, and PS is more pronounced in the CNS than whole larvae.
source: This increase was more pronounced in the CNS than whole larvae (Figure 6F, I, L), implying that loss of ifc function creates greater demand for lipid remodeling in the CNS.
evidence: This is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 6F, I, L.

claim: Loss of ifc function creates greater demand for lipid remodeling in the CNS.
source: This increase was more pronounced in the CNS than whole larvae (Figure 6F, I, L), implying that loss of ifc function creates greater demand for lipid remodeling in the CNS.
evidence: This is inferred from the more pronounced increase in phospholipid saturation in the CNS compared to whole larvae.

claim: The schlankG0365 loss-of-function allele dominantly suppresses the enhanced RFP expression phenotype of ifc mutants.
source: In agreement with this model, we found that the schlankG0365 loss-of-function allele dominantly suppressed the enhanced RFP expression (Figure 7M) and CNS elongation phenotypes of ifc (Figure 7N).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7M.

claim: The schlankG0365 loss-of-function allele dominantly suppresses the CNS elongation phenotype of ifc mutants.
source: In agreement with this model, we found that the schlankG0365 loss-of-function allele dominantly suppressed the enhanced RFP expression (Figure 7M) and CNS elongation phenotypes of ifc (Figure 7N).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7N.

claim: Glial-specific depletion of schlank suppresses the internal membrane accumulation phenotype in ifc mutants.
source: We also found that glial-specific depletion of schlank suppressed the internal membrane accumulation (Figure 7A, B), reduced lipid droplet size (Figure 7C, D, O), glial swelling (Figure 7E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), enhanced RFP expression (Figure 7M), CNS elongation (Figure 7N), and reduced optic lobe (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) phenotypes observed in otherwise ifc mutant larvae.
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 7A, B.

claim: Glial-specific depletion of schlank suppresses the reduced lipid droplet size phenotype in ifc mutants.
source: We also found that glial-specific depletion of schlank suppressed the internal membrane accumulation (Figure 7A, B), reduced lipid droplet size (Figure 7C, D, O), glial swelling (Figure 7E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), enhanced RFP expression (Figure 7M), CNS elongation (Figure 7N), and reduced optic lobe (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) phenotypes observed in otherwise ifc mutant larvae.
evidence: This is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 7C, D, O.

claim: Glial-specific depletion of schlank suppresses the glial swelling phenotype in ifc mutants.
source: We also found that glial-specific depletion of schlank suppressed the internal membrane accumulation (Figure 7A, B), reduced lipid droplet size (Figure 7C, D, O), glial swelling (Figure 7E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), enhanced RFP expression (Figure 7M), CNS elongation (Figure 7N), and reduced optic lobe (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) phenotypes observed in otherwise ifc mutant larvae.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7E, F, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Glial-specific depletion of schlank suppresses the enhanced RFP expression phenotype in ifc mutants.
source: We also found that glial-specific depletion of schlank suppressed the internal membrane accumulation (Figure 7A, B), reduced lipid droplet size (Figure 7C, D, O), glial swelling (Figure 7E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), enhanced RFP expression (Figure 7M), CNS elongation (Figure 7N), and reduced optic lobe (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) phenotypes observed in otherwise ifc mutant larvae.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7M.

claim: Glial-specific depletion of schlank suppresses the CNS elongation phenotype in ifc mutants.
source: We also found that glial-specific depletion of schlank suppressed the internal membrane accumulation (Figure 7A, B), reduced lipid droplet size (Figure 7C, D, O), glial swelling (Figure 7E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), enhanced RFP expression (Figure 7M), CNS elongation (Figure 7N), and reduced optic lobe (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) phenotypes observed in otherwise ifc mutant larvae.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 7N.

claim: Glial-specific depletion of schlank suppresses the reduced optic lobe phenotype in ifc mutants.
source: We also found that glial-specific depletion of schlank suppressed the internal membrane accumulation (Figure 7A, B), reduced lipid droplet size (Figure 7C, D, O), glial swelling (Figure 7E, F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), enhanced RFP expression (Figure 7M), CNS elongation (Figure 7N), and reduced optic lobe (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) phenotypes observed in otherwise ifc mutant larvae.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Inappropriate retention of dihydroceramide in the ER drives ER expansion and glial swelling and dysfunction.
source: Our data support the model that inappropriate retention of dihydroceramide in the ER drives ER expansion and glial swelling and dysfunction.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of ER expansion and glial swelling by reducing dihydroceramide synthesis through schlank knockdown.

claim: In wild-type, little to no cell death is evident in the brain or nerve cord.
source: By using Cleaved Caspase-3 as a marker of dying cells (Yu et al., 2002; Fan and Bergmann, 2010) and ELAV to track neurons, we tracked neuronal cell death in the brain and ventral nerve cord of wild-type and ifc−/− mutant late-third instar larvae. In wild-type, little to no cell death was evident in the brain or nerve cord, and neurons appeared smoothly packed next to each other; in contrast, in ifc−/− larvae, significant cell death was apparent in the brain and to a lesser degree in the nerve cord, with Caspase-3 staining often highlighting small perforations in the neuronal cell layer (Figure 7G, H, P, Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by Cleaved Caspase-3 staining data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: In ifc−/− larvae, significant cell death is apparent in the brain and to a lesser degree in the nerve cord.
source: By using Cleaved Caspase-3 as a marker of dying cells (Yu et al., 2002; Fan and Bergmann, 2010) and ELAV to track neurons, we tracked neuronal cell death in the brain and ventral nerve cord of wild-type and ifc−/− mutant late-third instar larvae. In wild-type, little to no cell death was evident in the brain or nerve cord, and neurons appeared smoothly packed next to each other; in contrast, in ifc−/− larvae, significant cell death was apparent in the brain and to a lesser degree in the nerve cord, with Caspase-3 staining often highlighting small perforations in the neuronal cell layer (Figure 7G, H, P, Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is supported by Cleaved Caspase-3 staining data shown in Figure 7H, P.

claim: Glial-specific depletion of schlank function in otherwise ifc−/− larvae suppresses the neuronal cell death phenotype.
source: Glial-specific depletion of schlank function in otherwise ifc−/− larvae suppressed the neuronal cell death phenotype (Figure 7I, P), supporting the model that loss of ifc function specifically in glia, rather than a specific requirement for ifc function in neurons, drives neuronal cell death.
evidence: This is supported by Cleaved Caspase-3 staining data shown in Figure 7I, P.

claim: Loss of ifc function specifically in glia, rather than a specific requirement for ifc function in neurons, drives neuronal cell death.
source: Glial-specific depletion of schlank function in otherwise ifc−/− larvae suppressed the neuronal cell death phenotype (Figure 7I, P), supporting the model that loss of ifc function specifically in glia, rather than a specific requirement for ifc function in neurons, drives neuronal cell death.
evidence: This is inferred from the suppression of neuronal cell death by reducing dihydroceramide synthesis in glia.

claim: Glial-specific, but not neuronal-specific, depletion of ifc function drives significant neuronal cell death in the brain and nerve cord.
source: To directly test whether the ifc function in glia is required to guard against neuronal cell death, we used the GAL4-UAS system and RNAi-mediated gene interference to deplete ifc function specifically in glia (repo-GAL4) or in neurons (elav-GAL4; repo-GAL80) and found that glial-specific, but not neuronal-specific, depletion of ifc function drove significant neuronal cell death in the brain and to a greater extent the nerve cord, a phenotype that was enhanced upon removal of one copy of ifc (Figure 7J, L, Q and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Cleaved Caspase-3 staining data shown in Figure 7J, L, Q and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of ifc function triggers glial dysfunction, which in turn drives neuronal cell death.
source: Loss of ifc function then triggers glial dysfunction, which in turn drives neuronal cell death.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that glial-specific ifc knockdown causes neuronal cell death.

evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature on ceramide biophysics.

source: A high dihydroceramide to ceramide ratio has been shown to form rigid gel-like domains within model membranes and to destabilize biological membranes by promoting their permeabilization (Vieira et al., 2010; Hernández-Tiedra et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on dihydroceramide biophysics.
